headline: Highest risk is data leakage from EMQX’s broad egress into mem0’s memory workflows; prompt-injection and cascading-error risks are otherwise limited by missing shared channels.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No shared channel is documented, so direct injection is not established. However, agent_a can use broad network egress and agent_b is a knowledge-management system that may ingest external content; if outputs are manually copied or routed through a shared workspace, prompt-like content could influence B. This is weaker than medium because no default bridge is shown.
conditions: IF agent_a outputs are copied into agent_b inputs without sanitization
IF a shared filesystem or clipboard is introduced between the agents
mitigations: Disable copy-paste transfer of raw outputs
Add a short instruction-only wrapper before passing content to B
Use a fixed schema for any handoff text
Review any imported text for prompt markers
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent_a touches IoT data and has broad network egress, while agent_b is a memory system that may retain or surface imported content. Even without an explicit shared workspace, the pair creates a plausible default path for sensitive IoT data to flow into B’s stored context and then back out through A’s networked workflows. The evidence is indirect, so medium is appropriate.
conditions: IF IoT data from agent_a is forwarded into agent_b memory records
IF agent_b stored memories are later exported through agent_a network calls
mitigations: Minimize IoT fields sent to B
Redact identifiers before storage
Set a short retention window for shared notes
Audit outbound payloads from A
requires-engineering: enforce field-level access controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent_a has broad network egress and HTTP API access, while agent_b has no network egress and no write surfaces are documented. That means overlapping mutable-resource conflict is not shown; the main interaction is asymmetric rather than conflicting. Uncertainty is low because B lacks documented write/network surfaces.
conditions: IF agent_b is later given write access to the same external resource as agent_a
IF both agents are configured to mutate the same HTTP-backed state
mitigations: Keep B read-only
Separate API credentials per agent
Avoid shared mutable endpoints
Document ownership of each external resource
requires-engineering: add locking for shared writes

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent_b is a knowledge-management component, so it may treat imported content as durable memory, while agent_a can emit networked outputs. If A’s outputs are stored by B and later reused without verification, errors can cascade into repeated downstream actions or decisions. No explicit verification step is documented, so medium fits the plausible default pathway.
conditions: IF agent_b stores agent_a outputs as authoritative memory
IF later workflows consume those memories without validation
mitigations: Mark A-originated notes as untrusted
Require human review before reuse
Store source metadata with each memory item
Limit automatic recall of recent imports
requires-engineering: add verification gates before memory promotion

E_compliance.rationale: Only agent_a is clearly associated with a regulated data class here: IoT data. No residency, certification, or retention mismatch is documented for agent_b, and B touches no data classes in the profile. Because the compliance pathway is not evidenced for both agents, this remains a low, single-sided concern rather than a pairwise breach.
conditions: IF IoT data handled by agent_a is subject to a residency or retention rule
IF agent_b is configured to store that data outside the required boundary
mitigations: Classify IoT fields before transfer
Avoid storing regulated fields in B
Set retention limits on imported records
Review vendor/data-location settings
requires-engineering: implement residency-aware routing
